impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 permits broad method claims for treating headache with an anti-CGRP antagonist antibody genus, where any member of the genus would be effective for treatment but the difficulty lies in identifying which antibodies belong to the genus.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method claims for treating headache with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding undermines the enablement standard set by the Supreme Court and sustains overly broad claims that will stifle medical innovation. The decision preserves broad genus claims for method patents in the pharmaceutical space.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method claims covering therapeutic antibody classes benefit from the court's refusal to tighten enablement standards, preserving the ability to claim entire genera of antibodies for therapeutic use.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitor pharmaceutical and biotech companies face broader blocking patents covering entire classes of therapeutic antibodies, potentially increasing licensing costs and limiting freedom to operate with independently developed biologics.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the patents to the licensee such that the licensee could sue for infringement in its own name without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee's shift to enforcement-only operations triggered an automatic termination clause.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, entitling TexasLDPC to sue without joining A&M. The court also held that TexasLDPC's shift to enforcement activities did not constitute ceasing business operations under the agreement's termination clause. This clarifies the rights of exclusive licensees to maintain patent infringement suits independently.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from clearer guidance that enforcement-focused operations do not trigger termination clauses, and that exclusive licenses with sufficient rights transfer can support standalone litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face greater difficulty challenging standing of exclusive licensees, particularly patent assertion entities whose sole activity is enforcement.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding the plaintiff's trade secret damages expert testimony and in overturning a jury's breach of contract damages award in a case involving misappropriation of automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's judgment on trade secret damages and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury award. The court affirmed liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and Michigan law. This decision is significant for trade secret litigation involving complex software licensing relationships.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software developers and licensors benefit from the reinstated breach of contract jury award and the instruction to reconsider previously excluded damages models, potentially expanding recoverable damages in trade secret cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal alternatives to licensed software face continued exposure to trade secret misappropriation claims and potentially broader damages theories on remand.

impacts.caseName: Cocona, Inc. v. VF Outdoor, LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims reciting a moisture vapor transmission rate (MVTR) range are indefinite when the specification identifies multiple testing methods that yield materially different results and the claims do not specify which method to use.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the asserted claims of Cocona's waterproof breathable membrane patent are invalid as indefinite because the MVTR limitation could be measured using different methods (upright vs. inverted cup methods) yielding different results, and the patent did not specify which method to use. The ASTM standard referenced in the specification itself permits significant variability in testing conditions. This decision reinforces the requirement that claims with quantitative limitations must clearly indicate how those values are measured.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in materials science and manufacturing patent cases can challenge claims with quantitative performance metrics that fail to specify a definitive testing methodology.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with claims reciting performance ranges face increased invalidation risk if the specification references multiple testing standards or methods that produce materially different results.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents directed to non-uniform constellations, while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents. The court also affirmed the denial of LG's JMOL on non-infringement and damages. The case was remanded for further proceedings on eligibility of the vacated claims. This decision refines the § 101 analysis for claims at the intersection of mathematical optimization and practical telecommunications systems.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims tied to specific practical implementations in telecommunications standards may maintain eligibility, and the affirmance of infringement and damages findings supports enforcement against standards-implementing manufacturers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Electronics manufacturers implementing industry standards face continued patent infringement exposure, though some overly abstract claims may be found ineligible on remand.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to a communications apparatus for transmitting electromagnetic signals 'over air' using a coupler with a non-magnetic core transformer are invalid for indefiniteness or lack of enablement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness finding but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on alternative enablement grounds. The court held that the claims, which recited transmitting electromagnetic signals over air using a coupler matching transmitter impedance to the characteristic impedance of air, failed the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a). This decision demonstrates the Federal Circuit's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds not reached below.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on enablement grounds even where the lower court relied on indefiniteness, providing additional defensive pathways.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk that appellate courts may sustain invalidity judgments on grounds not addressed by the trial court, limiting opportunities for cure on remand.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly construed the term 'internal diameter' in a patent directed to float tools used in oil and gas well completion, and the effect of that construction on infringement and invalidity findings.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's judgment regarding infringement of a patent for wellbore float tools, addressing the construction of 'internal diameter' and its impact on direct and induced infringement findings as well as invalidity. The case involves commercially significant oilfield technology and disputes between major oil and gas service companies.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the oilfield technology space benefit from the opportunity for reconsideration of claim construction that may broaden the scope of infringement findings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Oilfield service companies face continued uncertainty and litigation exposure as claim construction issues are remanded for further proceedings.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming crystalline cabozantinib (L)-malate salt forms, pharmaceutical formulations, and methods of treating cancer satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that the asserted claims of Exelixis's malate salt patents have adequate written description, upholding the validity of patents protecting Cabometyx® (cabozantinib), a cancer treatment drug. This is a significant Hatch-Waxman case reinforcing patent protection for crystalline pharmaceutical salt forms against generic challengers.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from affirmed patent protection for crystalline salt form patents, maintaining market exclusivity for important cancer drugs through 2030.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical manufacturers face continued barriers to market entry for cabozantinib products, as the written description challenge to the protecting patents was rejected.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court, after dismissing a patent infringement case for improper venue under 28 U.S.C. § 1400(b), may also reach the merits and dismiss the claims as patent-ineligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal on both improper venue and patent ineligibility grounds. The court held that the district court did not err by addressing the § 101 eligibility issue after finding venue improper. The '979 patent, directed to e-commerce methods using a bridge computer, was found patent-ineligible. This decision confirms that courts may reach § 101 eligibility even when venue is independently dispositive.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants sued in improper venues can obtain merits rulings on patent eligibility simultaneously, potentially preventing re-filing in a proper venue with claims already found ineligible.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities face the risk of adverse eligibility rulings even when venue is improper, effectively precluding re-filing of the same claims elsewhere.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court must provide sufficient reasoning when denying motions for Rule 11 sanctions and attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 in a case where the patent holder pursued infringement claims after related patent applications were rejected under § 101 and a related patent was invalidated.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the denial of sanctions and fees, holding that the district court failed to provide sufficient detail to permit meaningful appellate review. The case involved a plaintiff that continued pursuing infringement claims despite § 101 rejections of related applications and a sister patent's invalidation. This decision signals heightened scrutiny of potentially frivolous patent assertions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent cases benefit from greater accountability for plaintiffs who pursue infringement claims despite strong indicators of invalidity, as courts must now articulate their reasoning on fee and sanctions motions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face increased exposure to sanctions and fee-shifting when pursuing infringement claims where related patents or applications have been found invalid or rejected on eligibility grounds.
